prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a wide, flat ground plane sloping smoothly from the bright foreground within 1 metre up to a dark perimeter fence and trees roughly 15 to 30 metres away. In frames 1 and 2, three dogs in the central midground (roughly 4 to 10 metres away, spaced 1 to 3 metres apart) and distant people standing near the left and center fence (about 15 to 25 metres away) appear as small brighter silhouettes protruding above the ground gradient, while a nearby person partially enters the far-left edge within 1 metre in frame 2. In frame 3, as the camera pitches downward, a dark-and-tan dog approaches to within 1.5 to 2 metres directly in front and below eye level (facing forward/right toward the camera wearer's path), while two other dogs remain 8 to 10 metres behind to the upper-left and another dog is partly out of view on the far right. In frames 4 and 5, a white dog approaches from about 3 metres in front to roughly 1 to 1.5 metres on the left, coming nearly within arm's reach next to the camera wearer's own dark sleeve/hand or adjacent companion at the bottom-left corner (under 0.8 metres, partially occluded by the frame boundary). This map reveals the continuous ground distance gradient and separates dark dogs and the bottom-left foreground figure from the similarly dark mulch much clearer than RGB alone, though it becomes unreliable in frame 4 where overall brightness drops sharply as the ground tilts and in frame 5 where the fast-moving white dog's boundary blurs into the ground.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates discrete foreground and midground entities against the unlabelled black background of the fenced dog park, tracking their shifts from left to right across the 5-frame sequence. In frames 1 and 2, it detects a distant person near the center fence (about 20 metres away, facing roughly toward the field) and two people on the left (15 to 20 metres away), alongside midground dogs at 5 to 10 metres that are misclassified as 'sheep' and 'cow' spaced a few metres apart, while nothing is within the camera wearer's arm's reach except a partially visible person on the far-left edge of frame 2 and frame 4 (within 1 metre, heavily occluded by the left image border). In frame 3, a large green 'dog' mask captures the approaching dark-and-tan dog 1.5 to 2 metres in front and below the camera wearer, while a small brown 'person' mask marks a distant figure 12 to 15 metres behind it to the upper-left. In frames 4 and 5, as the camera tilts further downward and turns slightly right, a yellow mask tracks the white dog approaching from about 3 metres in the center-left to 1 to 1.5 metres on the left—nearly within arm's reach of the unlabelled arm/sleeve at the bottom-left—while misclassifying the dog as a 'bird'. While the masks help pinpoint tiny distant figures against the cluttered trees and fence that are hard to spot in RGB, the map is highly unreliable in its semantic class labels ('sheep', 'cow', 'bird' for dogs, and 'person' on a background dog in frame 3) and completely misses several visible dogs and background bystanders across the frames.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is almost entirely black across all five frames, failing to detect any human skeletons for the distant bystanders at 15 to 25 metres or for the partially visible person and arm at the bottom-left edge within 1 metre of the camera wearer. Its only output appears in frame 3, where a compact yellow body skeleton is erroneously fitted to the dark-and-tan dog situated 1.5 to 2 metres in front of and below the camera wearer. The false skeleton aligns with the dog's torso and lowered head angled toward the bottom-right, placing inferred head and upper-body keypoints near the dog's snout and shoulders while no magenta hand keypoints appear anywhere in the strip. Consequently, the pose map provides no usable information about which way actual people face, whether they look toward the camera wearer, or what is within anyone's arm's reach across the sequence. It offers no spatial insights beyond the RGB image and is completely unreliable here due to both false-positive human pose fitting on a quadruped and false-negative misses on all actual humans in the scene.
